scenarios.label: Heatwave
scenarios.description: Outdoor temperature +6 °C and base load +25% for three days, beyond anything in the forecaster's training window.

scenarios.label: Sensor dropout
scenarios.description: The forecast input freezes for two hours. The controller keeps acting on its last good estimate, which is what happens when a BMS point dies.

scenarios.label: Grid outage
scenarios.description: Grid import forced to zero for two hours; only critical load is served. The controller must ride through on thermal mass.

frontier.panel_d_note: Panel D is not monotonic, and that is the finding. Headroom without safety is not a benefit: persistence claims more capacity than climatology because its q95 simply follows the last observed value, and it then breaches the ceiling 87 times spending capacity that was never there. The like-for-like comparison is the static-margin study in eval/impact.py, which matches breach counts first and compares headroom second.

summary.statement: Held out entirely, the model scores 3.546 pinball on Fox_public_Denny against 2.576 for the same model trained on that building — +38%. It loses to seasonal naive (3.037), which is what the site could do on day one with no model. Coverage on the unseen building is 0.891 against a nominal 0.90.

transformer_upgrade_inr_per_kva.why: indicative turnkey cost of distribution transformer capacity in India, including civil and switchgear works. Order of magnitude only; a real society would price it from a quotation.

discount_rate.why: nominal discount rate for present-valuing a deferred capital outlay.

ev_load_growth_pct_per_year.why: compound annual growth in on-site EV charging energy. India's EV stock has been growing faster than this; 30% is deliberately conservative because a higher rate makes the deferral look better, not worse.

billing_months_per_year.why: the demand charge is a monthly maximum, so a month of saving annualises by twelve. This assumes June is a representative month, which it is not: it is the hottest, so this figure is an upper bound and is labelled as one.

buildings_per_feeder.why: commercial buildings of this size on one 11 kV distribution feeder. Stated as an assumption, not a survey.

feeders_per_discom.why: order of magnitude for a mid-sized state distribution utility.

static_margin.statement: A forecast-free static margin tuned to breach no more often than we do (p100, 0 breaches) leaves 198.1 kW usable. We leave 354.1 kW at 0 breaches. The forecast recovers 156.0 kW (+79%) of capacity at equal safety.

ev_headroom.deferral_statement: Uncoordinated charging breaches the ceiling at 220 kWh/day of EV load; ours holds to 500 kWh/day. At 30% annual growth in EV charging that gap is 3.1 years before the connection has to be upgraded.

tier3.annualised_caveat: the demand charge is a monthly maximum, so a month of saving annualises by twelve. This assumes June is a representative month, which it is not: it is the hottest, so this figure is an upper bound and is labelled as one.

avoided_capital.formula: contract kVA x INR/kVA, present-valued over the deferral

transformer_upgrade_inr_per_kva.why: indicative turnkey cost of distribution transformer capacity in India, including civil and switchgear works. Order of magnitude only; a real society would price it from a quotation.

discount_rate.why: nominal discount rate for present-valuing a deferred capital outlay.

tier4.arithmetic: saving per building per month x buildings per feeder x feeders per discom

feeders_per_discom.why: order of magnitude for a mid-sized state distribution utility.

tier4.note: This is arithmetic, not a market size. It assumes every building on every feeder is like this one, has a demand charge, and is instrumented. The point of the multiplication is the shape of the number, not its precision.

model.model_card:
# Model card — LightGBM quantile (ours)

**Building:** `Fox_office_Gaylord`  
**Role in the system:** primary — its q95 enters the capacity constraint  
**Generated by:** `eval/model_cards.py` from `results/forecast_benchmark_Fox_office_Gaylord.json`

## Purpose

Probabilistic 15-minute forecast of the building's uncontrollable base load, direct multi-horizon out to 16 hours, reported as the quantiles 0.05, 0.25, 0.50, 0.75 and 0.95.

The output is not a chart for a human to look at. It is a numerical bound inside a hard constraint in an optimiser:

```
base_q95[t] + controllable[t] - solar_q05[t]  <=  D_target
```

Every kilowatt of forecast error is a kilowatt of headroom the building either wastes or dangerously gives away.

## Data

Building Data Genome Project 2 — real hourly electricity meter data plus site weather, upsampled to 15 minutes with a shape-preserving PCHIP interpolation. Site Fox (Tempe, Arizona), selected as the hottest site in the set and a reasonable solar-geometry analogue for northern India.

| Block | Range | (origin, horizon) rows |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Train | 2016-01-01 00:00 to 2017-03-31 23:45 | see `splits` in the JSON |
| Calibrate | 2017-04-01 00:00 to 2017-05-31 23:45 | |
| Test (touched once) | 2017-06-01 00:00 to 2017-06-30 23:45 | 184,320 |

The split is temporal and frozen in `forecast/splits.py`. It is never random: neighbouring 15-minute samples of a load series are almost the same number, so a random split is a memory test. `tests/test_leakage.py` asserts the ordering and, separately, rewrites the future of the series and asserts that no feature at an earlier origin moves.

## Features

30 features, all knowable at the forecast origin:

- lags at 1, 2, 4, 8, 96, 192, 672 steps before the origin
- rolling mean and standard deviation over 1 hour, 1 day and 1 week
- same-time-of-day mean over the trailing four weeks
- outdoor temperature at the origin, and its 1-hour change
- horizon index (one model serves every horizon)
- calendar: time of day, day of week, weekend, US federal holiday, day of year
- a solar elevation term

**One declared exception to origin-time causality:** weather at the target time is used as a perfect forecast. This flatters the model and is stated here rather than discovered. It can be stressed with `--weather-noise-c`, and the `sensor_dropout` scenario freezes the forecast entirely.

## Training

LightGBM with `objective='quantile'`, one booster per quantile, early stopping on the calibration block.

| Hyperparameter | Value |
| --- | --- |
| `objective` | quantile |
| `metric` | quantile |
| `learning_rate` | 0.06 |
| `num_leaves` | 63 |
| `min_data_in_leaf` | 200 |
| `feature_fraction` | 0.85 |
| `bagging_fraction` | 0.85 |
| `bagging_freq` | 1 |
| `lambda_l2` | 1.0 |
| `num_threads` | 8 |
| `num_boost_round` (cap) | 600 |

Best iteration per quantile: q05 = 472, q25 = 178, q50 = 175, q75 = 143, q95 = 199.

## Calibration

Two stages, both fitted on the calibration block and never on test.

1. **Split conformal.** Each quantile is shifted by the empirical residual quantile, per horizon. Gradient-boosted quantile regression is not calibrated by construction; without this the nominal level is decorative.
2. **Adaptive conformal (ACI).** Split conformal fitted on April–May undercovers in June because June is hotter — ordinary distribution shift. ACI moves the offset against the realised exceedance rate after each target time becomes known, which buys a distribution-free, finite-sample coverage property rather than an assumed one.

The same layer is applied to every baseline in the benchmark, so the comparison measures the forecast rather than the wrapper.

## Evaluation

Measured once on the test block, on data the model never saw.

| Metric | Calibrated | Raw model |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Mean pinball loss (kW) | **2.397** | 2.900 |
| CRPS (kW, five-level approximation) | 4.922 | 5.847 |
| Winkler score, 90% interval | 51.7 | 70.6 |
| 90% interval coverage | **0.891** | 0.707 |
| Actuals at or below q95 | 0.939 | 0.833 |
| Mean interval width (kW) | 39.6 | 26.0 |
| Calibration error | 0.0068 | 0.0785 |
| PIT deviation from flat | 0.0234 | 0.1879 |
| MAE of the median (kW) | 7.03 | 8.19 |
| RMSE of the median (kW) | 9.73 | 11.42 |

Point accuracy is reported because it is always asked for. It is not the operative metric here: the controller substitutes q95 into a hard constraint, so what matters is whether q95 is really a 95th percentile and how tight it is while staying so.

Against the full benchmark and the ablation: see `results/forecast_benchmark.md` and `results/ablation.md`.

### Rolling origin

8 expanding-window folds. Pinball 2.987 ± 1.294 (worst fold 5.429), coverage 0.913 with a worst fold of 0.874. Best of the field on 7 of 8 folds.

### What the model uses

Mean |SHAP| on held-out data, q95 booster: `hod_cos`, `dow_sin`, `solar_elev`, `cdd_fut`, `rmean_672`, `t_out_fut`.

### What the model needs

Drop a feature group, retrain, measure the damage (600,000 rows, 250 rounds, scored on validation).

| Group removed | Pinball | Degradation |
| --- | --- | --- |
| calendar | 6.408 | +4.096 (+177.2%) |
| weather forecast | 3.097 | +0.785 (+34.0%) |
| daily and weekly lags | 2.330 | +0.018 (+0.8%) |
| weather now | 2.289 | -0.023 (-1.0%) |
| recent lags | 2.283 | -0.029 (-1.3%) |
| rolling statistics | 2.154 | -0.158 (-6.8%) |

## Known limitations

- **The building is American.** Load *shapes* are American: this site peaks around 14:00, inside the tariff's normal window rather than the 18:00–22:00 peak window, so the time-of-day arbitrage available here is weaker than it would be for an Indian office. The result is conservative rather than flattering, but the reader should know.
- **Hourly source data upsampled to 15 minutes.** Interpolation smooths real sub-hourly variability, so measured peaks are understated.
- **Weather at the target time is a perfect forecast.** Stated above.
- **The base load / HVAC split is inferred, not submetered.** The meter is one channel; the decomposition is a model.
- **One month of test data.** June 2017, the hottest month at the site. The rolling-origin folds exist because one month is not a season.
- **Calibration is a property of the test distribution.** ACI recovers coverage under drift but it recovers it *after* the drift starts; the first few intervals of a regime change are the exposed ones.

## Intended use

- Supplying the upper bound `base_q95` to the demand-ceiling constraint of the
  chance-constrained MILP in `control/mpc.py`, at 15-minute resolution out to
  16 hours.
- Supplying `q50` to the energy-cost term of the same optimiser, where planning
  on a tail would overstate the bill and distort the trade-off.
- Reporting rolling coverage in the operator interface, so the safety property is
  monitored rather than assumed.

## Not intended for

- Billing, settlement or any figure a consumer is charged on. The bill engine in
  `tariff/bill.py` is the only source of money in this system, and it reads
  realised meter data, never a forecast.
- Buildings materially unlike the training site without re-fitting. The
  cold-start study measures what happens on a building held out entirely; read
  it before assuming transfer.
- Horizons beyond 16 hours. The model was neither trained nor calibrated
  there and the controller clamps its planning horizon rather than extrapolating.
- Any decision where a 5% exceedance rate is unacceptable. q95 is a 95th
  percentile by construction and by measurement; it is not a guarantee that load
  will never exceed it, and the controller is designed around that fact.

## Reproducing

```bash
./reproduce.sh          # everything, from raw data to figures
python eval/forecast_eval.py --buildings Fox_office_Gaylord   # just this table
```

Seeds are fixed. Every number above was written by a script; if this card disagrees with `results/`, `results/` is right and this card is stale.
